title: The foolishness of the cross (1 Corinthians 1:18–25)
hook: the foolishness of God is wiser than men

segments.voice: Yesterday, reasonable service, the living sacrifice of Romans 12. Your line was rejoice and weep with them.

On the Palatine Hill in Rome, archaeologists found a drawing scratched on an ancient plaster wall. It shows a figure on a cross with the head of a donkey, and a young man raising a hand toward it. Underneath, in rough Greek: Alexamenos worships his god. It's a joke, somebody's mockery of a Christian: worshiping a crucified man was ridiculous enough to draw. Paul would not have been surprised by it at all.
screen: `A SCRATCH ON A ROMAN WALL.` → `A CRUCIFIED FIGURE, MOCKED.` → `ALEXAMENOS WORSHIPS HIS GOD.`

segments.voice: Now to Paul's letters to Corinth, a rich, proud, quarrelsome port city. The church there is divided, and some members prize clever speech and wisdom. So Paul starts at the hardest point. In the Douay-Rheims: "For the word of the cross, to them indeed that perish, is foolishness; but to them that are saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God." The Greek word for foolishness is moria, folly. Yes, Paul is saying, to plenty of listeners this sounds absurd. A crucified Messiah. A God who wins by losing. To some, a stumbling block; to others, foolishness. He doesn't make it sound more respectable. He turns it around: "For the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men." Then, with a smile, he tells the Corinthians to look at themselves: not many of you were wise by worldly standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth. God chose what the world counts foolish and weak. The mocking drawing and Paul's letter agree on one thing: from the outside, the cross looks absurd. Paul's claim is that the absurd thing is exactly where God chose to show his power. Catholic churches set a crucifix on or near the altar: the very image the mocker drew, now held up without embarrassment.
screen: `CORINTH, PROUD OF ITS WISDOM.` · `MORIA: FOOLISHNESS.` · `A GOD WHO WINS BY LOSING.` · `NOT MANY WISE, NOT MANY MIGHTY.` · then, large: `THE FOOLISHNESS OF GOD IS WISER.`

segments.voice: Think of a kindness that looks a little silly by the world's math: letting someone have the parking spot, paying for the coffee behind you, spending time with someone who can't do anything for you, forgiving a debt. Picture doing it, and someone shaking their head, and let that be fine. If you pray, look at a crucifix or picture one, and remember how foolish it looked.
Moria. Greek for folly: Paul's word for how the crucified Messiah sounded to the world, and the heart of what Paul would not soften. Today's word.
Your line: foolish and wise. The cross once looked like a joke on a wall. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholic churches place a crucifix on or near the altar, Catholics often wear or hang one at home, and on Good Friday the faithful come forward to venerate the cross.

trapdoor: what you thought: the cross was always a respected religious symbol.
what it means: in Paul's world it was a mark of total shame, and he says God chose exactly that to show his power and wisdom.

what a scholar hears: Paul names two reactions, a stumbling block to some and foolishness to others, and answers both with the power and wisdom of God. the Alexamenos graffito shows the second reaction scratched into a wall.

chat.says: Didn't early Christians feel embarrassed worshiping someone who was crucified?
options: Paul admits the cross sounds like folly to many, and calls it God's power anyway.
No, everyone in Rome saw crucifixion as a noble, honorable way to die.
Yes, so Paul softened it and stressed Jesus's wise teaching over the cross.
chat.meaning: Paul doesn't make the cross respectable: to some it's moria, folly, but the foolishness of God is wiser than men.

notes: Confirm KJV wording of 1 Corinthians 1:18 and 1:25.

Verse 1:23 ('unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness') is deliberately paraphrased as 'to some, a stumbling block; to others, foolishness' to avoid any framing against Jewish listeners; a Keeper may prefer the full verse.
Alexamenos graffito: dates proposed range from the late 1st to the early 3rd century; 'probably around the year two hundred' hedged. Confirm.
Moron from Greek mōros: standard etymology; confirm.
Crucifixion rarely depicted before the 5th century (e.g. Santa Sabina doors): confirm.
